passage:
Subject: Something at work
Dear Naveen,
When we worked on the audit team you told me to write if things got difficult, so here goes. On Monday, in the review with the regional head and five others, my senior, Mr Kulkarni, presented the pricing model I built as “my approach.” He looked at the slide the whole time and never at me. I said nothing. I sat there with my face hot, angry and strangely helpless. Afterwards two colleagues quietly told me they knew it was mine, but nobody spoke in the meeting. I don't want to confront him in public. I've started a dated file of what I contribute, and I'll show him the next draft early with a short note to the team. Does that sound sensible?
Disha

qa.q: What did Mr Kulkarni call the pricing model in the review?
qa.a: Mr Kulkarni called it “my approach.”

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as Disha sat through the review?
qa.a: Disha felt angry and helpless, with a hot face, and stayed silent in front of the regional head and five others.

qa.q: What steps does Disha plan instead of a public confrontation?
qa.a: Disha has started a dated file of contributions and plans to show the next draft early with a short note to the team.

qa.q: How might the two colleagues who quietly said they knew it was Disha's have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt uneasy about not speaking up in the meeting, which fits telling Disha afterwards in private.

grounding: A junior finds their work presented as a senior's idea, feels anger and helplessness and chooses to document contributions and speak early.

passage: So, the worst moment? Honestly, a Wednesday. I'm Lavanya, and I had spent three weekends on a customer-survey design. In the client call, my manager Ganga said, “Here is the approach I've developed,” and clicked to my slide. Seven people on that call, and nobody looked at me because nobody knew it was mine. I was so angry my hands went cold, and I couldn't think of a single thing to say that wouldn't sound petty. That night I emailed myself the dates and drafts. From then on my weekly update named exactly what I was working on, and in the next planning meeting I spoke early: “I'll present the survey design.” Ganga blinked, then said, “Good. Go ahead.”

qa.q: How many people were on the client call?
qa.a: Seven people were on the call.

qa.q: Why couldn't Lavanya think of anything to say during the call?
qa.a: Lavanya was so angry that hands went cold, and feared that anything said would sound petty in front of the client.

qa.q: What did Lavanya change after that night, and why was it a safer choice than confronting in public?
qa.a: Lavanya kept dated records, named the work in the weekly update and claimed the presentation early, which made ownership clear without embarrassing Ganga in front of a client.

qa.q: What might Ganga have been thinking when Ganga blinked at Lavanya's early claim?
qa.a: Ganga was probably surprised and may have realised that Lavanya's work was now visible, so agreeing with “Good. Go ahead.” was the easy way to respond.

grounding: A junior finds their work presented as a senior's idea, feels anger and helplessness and chooses to document and speak up early.

passage:
Subject: Follow-up on the route-planning idea
Hi Ramesh,
Thanks for presenting the delivery route plan at Monday's team meeting; it's great the regional head liked it. I wanted to raise something early, before the next review. The model and the three-zone idea came from my analysis of 4 March, which I sent you by email along with the spreadsheet (both attached). In the meeting it came across as your idea, and a few colleagues asked me afterwards why I hadn't contributed. Honestly, that left me frustrated and a bit invisible.
I'd like my part to be visible. Could we present it together at Friday's review, or could you mention my analysis when you send the summary to the regional head?
Happy to talk in person today if that's easier.
Best,
Samir

qa.q: On what date did Samir do the analysis?
qa.a: On 4 March.

qa.q: How did Samir feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Samir felt frustrated and invisible, especially when colleagues asked why Samir hadn't contributed.

qa.q: Why is Samir's email a safer choice than confronting Ramesh in the meeting?
qa.a: It is calm, attaches proof, raises the issue early and offers practical fixes, so Ramesh can correct it without a public fight.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading the email?
qa.a: Ramesh may feel caught out and a little defensive, but the polite tone gives an easy way to share the credit.

grounding: A junior whose analysis was presented as a senior's idea documents the contribution and raises it early and calmly.

passage: So, Bhavna, you want the real story for your podcast on workplaces? Fine. I'm Nirmala, and back then I was a junior researcher at an NGO. I spent six weeks on a survey of street vendors. Our programme head presented it to the donors as 'my field insight'. I sat at the back of the hall, clapping like everyone else, and my hands were shaking. I wanted to stand up and say, 'That's mine!' But who'd believe a junior over a head? I went home feeling sick and useless. My friend told me to write it all down. So I made a timeline: dates, emails, draft versions. The next week I asked the head for a meeting and calmly showed it. The final report had my name as co-author. I still get angry thinking about that evening, though.

qa.q: How long did Nirmala spend on the survey?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel sitting at the back while the head presented?
qa.a: Nirmala felt angry and helpless, hands shaking, wanting to speak up but doubting anyone would believe a junior.

qa.q: Which step got Nirmala credited, and why did it work?
qa.a: Writing a timeline of dates, emails and drafts, then calmly showing it in a private meeting; the evidence was hard to deny and no one was publicly shamed.

qa.q: How might the programme head have felt seeing the timeline?
qa.a: The head was likely uncomfortable and caught out, but the calm, private meeting made it easier to agree to co-authorship.

grounding: A junior whose survey is presented as a senior's insight feels angry and helpless, then documents the work and raises it calmly.

passage: Monday: in the design review, Maria presented the cooling fix for the new machine as 'something I've been working on'. Joseph had built it over three weekends. He stared at the table, his face hot, while the plant manager congratulated her. His colleague Dilip glanced at him and said nothing. Wednesday: Joseph wanted to email the whole department. Instead he took Dilip's advice, pulled out his dated sketches and test logs, and asked Maria for fifteen minutes. 'I'd like the review notes to show my part,' he said, his voice steady though his hands weren't. Maria went quiet, then said, 'You're right. I got carried away.' The next Monday: the revised review notes listed Joseph as lead on the cooling fix. Dilip gave him a thumbs-up across the floor.

qa.q: How long had Joseph worked on the cooling fix?
qa.a: Over three weekends.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling during Monday's review?
qa.a: He felt angry and helpless, staring at the table with a hot face while Maria took the praise.

qa.q: Why was Joseph's Wednesday approach wiser than emailing the whole department?
qa.a: He used dated sketches and test logs and spoke to Maria privately and early, which let her correct it without a public fight.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilip watching all this?
qa.a: Dilip sees the credit-taking and stays quiet at first, then helps with advice and is pleased when Joseph gets the credit.

grounding: Over a week a junior moves from anger at a senior taking credit to calmly raising it with documented evidence.

passage: Mehak, you think this only happens to you? Sit. When I was twenty-four, at the survey office in Pune, I built a whole new sampling plan, three weeks of late nights. At the review meeting my senior, Mr Khanna, stood up and presented it as "an idea I've been developing". Six people nodded. I sat there with my hands shaking under the table, so angry I couldn't taste my tea. I wanted to stand up and shout. My friend Leela pressed her foot on mine. Afterwards she said, "Shout today and you're the difficult girl for ten years." So I went home and wrote down dates, drafts, every email with my name on the file. On the next project I sent my plan to the whole team on day one. Nobody could borrow that one. That is how your Nirmala Aunty learnt, beta.

qa.q: How long had young Nirmala worked on the sampling plan?
qa.a: She spent three weeks of late nights building it.

qa.q: What was young Nirmala feeling when Mr Khanna presented her plan?
qa.a: She was angry and helpless, her hands shaking under the table, so upset she couldn't taste her tea.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Nirmala protected her work?
qa.a: Instead of shouting, she recorded dates, drafts and emails, and on the next project sent her plan to the whole team on day one.

qa.q: Why might Leela have pressed her foot on Nirmala's in the meeting?
qa.a: Leela was worried a public outburst would get her friend labelled difficult for years and wanted to protect her.

grounding: Nirmala Aunty recalls a senior presenting her work as his, and learning that documenting and sharing early is safer than a public confrontation.
